title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2
text:
Goals Going In
This was the first race of the season. I had not even done a parkrun yet, so I had very little sense of where my race fitness actually stood.
Because of that, the goal was to put in a solid effort without going too deep into the red. The problem was that I did not really know where that red line was yet, and I did not want to turn the day into a long suffer-fest by crossing it too early and then spending the rest of the race hanging on.
Even so, I did have some minimum targets in mind:

about 800m in the swim
10km on the bike
16 laps on the run

title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2
text:
Swim
I started in the fifth wave. This time the swim was in the 50m pool, which I like. Even though I am not especially used to that length, it lets you settle into a rhythm instead of constantly breaking it with turns and push-offs every few seconds.
I shared the lane with a much younger guy who looked fit, and in the next lane there was another athlete who looked competitive and possibly in my age group. I kept an eye on both of them, but without trying to chase too hard. There is no drafting advantage here, so there is no point burning matches just to sit on someone’s feet.
In the end, I did not need to worry too much about either of them, or really anyone else in my wave. I out-swam everybody in the wave by at least one lap, which was a first for me. I do not think that means I suddenly became a great swimmer overnight. More likely, this particular wave just was not that strong in the water. Still, it was a nice feeling to be clear of everyone.
I finished on exactly 800m, with about 10 seconds to spare. That works out to roughly 1:52 per 100m, so not especially quick. Pretty leisurely, really.
But that was not the point. The important thing for me was that I hit my minimum target of 800m and did it while feeling completely under control. It stayed aerobic the whole way through. I was just focused on staying calm, breathing comfortably, and holding something close to decent form.









The swim pace starts off reasonably well, at a little over 1:30 per 100m, but it quickly fades toward 1:50 and at times even slower. That happens alongside a small but noticeable increase in stroke rate, from below 29 to above 30. It is not a huge jump, but it is there, and to me it suggests a breakdown in form: quicker and shorter strokes, but clearly less efficient ones.
Through all of that, heart rate stays fairly low, around 125 bpm, which matches the feeling I had in the water: controlled, comfortable, and never close to the limit.
In other words, the data confirms something I already know very well: my main limiter in the swim is technique, not aerobic capacity.

title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2
text:
Bike
The bike was a similar story. Because it is stationary, you do not really get much feedback on what the other competitors are doing, so there is not much point in trying to race off other people. My focus was simply to sit around 40km/h, which would get me to 10km by the end of the segment, while making sure it never felt like I had to fight to stay there.
I definitely pushed harder on the bike than I did in the swim. I am much more comfortable judging effort on two wheels than I am in the water, and in general I know myself better on dry land. Even so, the effort still felt controlled. My legs were not burning, my breathing was not ragged, and I was never in that place where you are just staring at the clock and begging for the 15 minutes to end.
To keep up the tradition of messing up at least one leg of the race, I forgot to start my watch for the bike, so I do not have a complete set of heart-rate data to analyze afterward.
I finished on 10.3km, with a few seconds to spare. Not enough to get to 10.5km and collect the next bump in points, but still enough to hit the target I had in mind.
So again, mission accomplished, both in terms of distance and in terms of keeping the effort where I wanted it.

title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2
text:
Run
The run is probably the leg I could have raced a bit better.
Once again, my main guide was feel: stay comfortable, stay in control, do not push so hard that the whole thing unravels. I was also glancing at pace, but that is not especially useful indoors because the watch is all over the place. By the end it measured about 200m more than the official distance, which is a full extra lap. Power would probably have been a better metric, but I do not have a good reference yet for what kind of running power I should be targeting in this format.
From the start, it felt like a three-man race: the young guy from my swim lane, the other athlete I thought might be in my age group, and me.
The younger guy went out hard right away. I let him go immediately. That pace was not part of my plan, and probably not something I could have held even if I had wanted to. More importantly, he was not in my age group, so I was not really racing him anyway. My attention was much more on the other guy, the one I thought might be my real competition.
We ran together for about the first 10 laps. At times he was slightly ahead, then I was. During that stretch we also reeled in the younger guy, which confirmed that his opening pace had been too ambitious.
After about 10 laps, the maybe-my-age-group guy put in a surge and ended up covering half a lap more than I did. Maybe, just maybe, I could have gone with him. But I was not convinced that this was the right race to make that move.
This is where race strategy matters. Yes, he beat me by half a lap on the run, but I knew I had swum much better than him. The bike was less certain, but I trusted my bike strength and thought it was unlikely that he would put enough time into me there to undo the swim advantage.
And in the end, it turned out that he was not even in my age group after all. He was in the younger 30-39 category.









Even though the effort felt controlled, heart rate went quite a bit higher than I would have liked. That is a bit of a concern, because I do not think I can sustain much more than that for very long, which in turn suggests I may not have much room to go faster yet.
The hopeful interpretation is that this was simply the first real race effort of the season. Because of snow and ice, I had almost no opportunities to do proper fast running sessions through the winter, so it makes sense that the system was not fully ready for that kind of work yet.
On the positive side, all the metrics are fairly consistent. There is no major drop in pace or power, which suggests that the elevated heart rate was still reasonably well tolerated, even if it was higher than I wanted.
The little jump in power and the quicker pace toward the end was deliberate: I wanted to make sure I got through the 16th lap in time and secured all the available points for that distance.

title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2
text:
Final thoughts
Even if this ended up being my worst result in terms of ranking, I am happy with the approach. I performed almost at the same level as in previous indoor races, but I did it feeling much more in control and at a lower perceived effort. Whether I already have the ability to push significantly harder and still sustain it is not clear yet, but this still feels like a promising sign for the season ahead.
That matters because the real goal this year is bigger: qualify for the 2027 Sprint Duathlon World Championship.
On that note, the swim is obviously not the priority this season. Still, the data showed a pattern I know very well: I struggle to sustain pace in the water. The good news is that, with the main focus shifting toward competitive cycling and running rather than swimming, I can afford to slow things down in the pool and focus much more on technique for the rest of the year, with the hope of coming back stronger next season.

Quick Recap of the Format
In this series, your score is based on how far you can swim, bike, and run in 15 minutes each. The further you go, the more points you earn. The series includes four races, but only your best three results count toward the final standings. Whoever has the highest point total at the end wins the championship (and gets a pretty cool trophy). Age Group athletes can also earn bragging rights—and a digital certificate—if they top their 10-year age group.

title: Meadowale Parkrun
text:
Race Overview
This was the first proper run test of the season.
That sounds more structured than it really was. I had done little to no speed work beforehand. The only remotely hard running in the bank was the 15-minute run segment at Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 2 two weeks earlier.
Beyond that, winter in Canada had done a good job of shutting down any grand plans for sharp 5K-specific preparation. It is hard enough to run consistently outside through the colder months. It is even harder to do anything fast when every session risks becoming a negotiation with snow, slush, or ice. As a side note, I will probably be looking for a treadmill before next winter.


Before the Start
This test had already been pushed back two or three times because of icy conditions. There is not much point calling it a fitness test if a quarter of your mental energy is going into staying upright.
The goal was simple: ideally break 22 minutes, put in a solid shift, but do not force it.
The pacing plan was conservative on paper. Start at about 4:20/km, settle there, and then maybe squeeze things down near the end if the legs were still cooperating. Holding 4:20/km would give a finish of roughly 21:40, which meant I had about 20 seconds of margin even if things got a bit ragged late on.
My warm-up was also flawless in the way that only bad warm-ups can be: I arrived about 0 minutes before the start.
Even with that, there was still just enough time to study the opposition. A couple of guys looked quick. One in particular stood out immediately: old muddy shoes, holes in the running tights, cycling top. You see that combination and you know the man is not here for a gentle jog around the park.


How It Went
From the gun, the plan was to feel like I was holding back.
Two guys went out hard straight away, including the one I had already marked down as suspiciously serious. I let them go without hesitation. Then I looked at the watch: 4:10/km.
That was clearly faster than the plan, but it still felt under control, so I made a small adjustment. Rather than forcing myself back to 4:20/km, I decided to hold something in the 4:10 to 4:15/km range and see how long that remained sensible.
For a while, the effort felt good. I could also hear the footsteps of another runner tucked in behind me, close enough to be noticed the whole time, but I stayed on my own pace and ignored it.
Toward the end of kilometre 3, the first signs of fatigue started to show. The pace slipped, but not dramatically, only by a few seconds per kilometre. Two more runners came past me at that point, and I did not try, or perhaps could not try, to go with them.
Then came the moment every 5K seems to require: a quick negotiation with yourself. I glanced at the watch and saw 4:30/km. That was a bit too charitable. Slipping back to 4:20/km would have been acceptable. 4:30/km was not. So the internal instruction was simple: pick it up.
I finished in 20:49.
That felt like a good result for late March, especially with so little specific speed work in the legs. More importantly, it did not feel like a full all-out effort. There is clearly more in there somewhere. The next job is figuring out how to access it.


What the Data Says
The basic summary is reassuring enough. The average pace comes out at just over 4:13/km, with heart rate and power both building to sensible 5K levels rather than exploding early.
The chart below tells the story in some more detail. Pace was strong early, then drifted in the second half as the effort started to bite. Heart rate rises steadily, which is what you would expect in a properly paced 5K. Cadence stays fairly stable, so the slowdown looks more like a drop in force production than a complete collapse in mechanics.









The kilometre averages make that progression easier to read. The first three kilometres are the strongest part of the race. After that, pace gives away a few seconds while power, cadence, and heart rate all stay reasonably high. That fits the subjective feeling quite well: I was tiring, but not blowing up.

text:
Last 5K prep test before the World Championships
Lately, my running training zones for heart rate, pace, and power have been completely out of sync. With just five weeks to go before the World Championships, my coach threw another test my way — a chance to reset the numbers and see exactly where I stand. The goal was simple on paper: match (or better) my last Parkrun effort, but with smarter pacing. The plan was to open the first 3K between 4:10 and 4:15/km, then gradually turn the screws. Easy, right? Well, not quite. A couple of days before the race I came down with something and lined up on the start feeling far from 100%. Still, the first half went almost perfectly. I kept things controlled at 4:07, 4:09, 4:09 — a big improvement from my previous attempt where I went out way too hot. The challenge came in the final stretch. The negative splits I had in mind slipped away as fatigue kicked in, and I slowed to 4:15 and 4:18 for the last 2K. The end result? Practically identical to last time — just three seconds slower, which, given the circumstances, I’ll take as a small win. The only sting in the tail was watching another runner in my category fly past me right near the end to grab first place, crossing the line eight seconds ahead. A tough pill to swallow, but another reminder that pacing — and finishing strong — makes all the difference.

text:
Testing the Legs at Parkrun – With a Dash of Triathlon Prep
This morning’s mission: a 5K parkrun to fine-tune my training zones and see just how ready (or not!) I am for the Sprint Triathlon Age Group World Championship in Wollongong.
Lately, running and I haven’t exactly been best friends. I’ve been slogging through a series of 22-minute-plus 5Ks, and with a brand-new coach in my corner (more on that drama soon), I was curious—could I sneak under 22 minutes again? Maybe even flirt with 21?
This was my debut at this particular parkrun venue. It’s one of those Goldilocks events: popular enough for a buzz, but not so packed that you spend the whole time dodging elbows. The course is a flat, three-lap loop around a pond—no hills, no hairpin turns, just you, your legs, and the clock. Basically, a recipe for speed… if you don’t get carried away.
Which I promptly did.
I blasted off way too hard, hitting 4:50/km for the first 2K, fully aware I’d lit the matchbook a little too soon. I tucked in behind a speedy young woman for a while, but she eventually glided away like it was nothing. My pace crept above 4:20/km, but mercifully the finish line was getting close. A few runners caught me, but I crossed in 20:39—comfortably under my goal and my fastest 5K since 2016. Not exactly Olympic-qualifying stuff, but for me, a sweet little victory.
Post-race, the parkrun magic kicked in. That friendly, chatty vibe is one of the reasons I love these events. Several people came over to ask about my St. Albans Striders vest, which turned into some great conversations.
So now, with my confidence slightly restored and my legs reminded they can still turn over quickly, it’s back to the grind. Wollongong is calling.

title: Gravenhurst Sprint Triathlon
text:
Photo by Chappell Digital.


This race report comes from my experience at the Gravenhurst Triathlon, my first outdoor race of the season. While it was technically a “C” race (meaning lower priority), let’s be honest - what athlete doesn’t want to perform their best, regardless of the race’s status? Even though my AI coach Hugo from HumanGo had me deep in base training (far from peak season, with my A-race coming in October), I was excited to test my fitness.
Talk about challenging conditions! The universe seemed determined to make this interesting: I caught a bug on Wednesday that knocked me out of training for a couple of days, had to wake up at the ungodly hour of 3:15 AM to get there, and - just to add some spice - there were wildfires in the area making the air quality questionable. Not exactly the perfect recipe for a stellar performance!
Still, I had some specific goals I was eager to tackle:

Test my improved swimming (spoiler: well, that was humbling)
Attempt flying mounts and dismounts on the bike (adventure ensued)
Rock the official Team Canada racing kit (because looking fast counts, right?)
Try out my shiny new Garmin Forerunner 965 (RIP trusty Fenix 5Plus)




Early morning view of the lake.


Let me paint you a picture of Gravenhurst - it’s this charming village in Ontario’s Muskoka region, not far from Bracebridge (where I’ve raced twice before) and my in-laws’ cottage. The swim takes place in Muskoka Lake, and despite my early-June temperature concerns, we lucked out with a comfortable 18°C water temperature.
Now, here’s where things get interesting - this race has a unique twist. Instead of your typical beach start, you get to jump off a cruise boat in the middle of the lake. Cool, right? Well, the boat had other plans, causing a 20-minute delay. At this point, I was starting to wonder if someone had broken a mirror at race headquarters.



3-2-1 JUMP! Photo by Chappell Digital.


When we finally got going, the swim was straightforward - a direct shot to the dock following a line of buoys. The first 100 meters felt like a washing machine with arms and legs everywhere, but things settled down after that. I focused on maintaining good form and staying “long” in the water. Despite these noble intentions, my 750m time of 15:41 (2:09/100m pace) was… let’s just say it wasn’t setting any records. My Garmin data showed some decent patches mixed with what looked like underwater sightseeing - clearly, there’s still plenty of room for improvement in my swimming!
T1 featured a lengthy run-up (perfect for wetsuit stripping), but I made my first tactical error here - skipping my usual half gel and not taking any nutrition on the bike. This would come back to haunt me later.
The flying mount attempt was, well, less “flying” and more “controlled stumbling.” While I managed to start with my feet clipped in, getting them into the actual shoes was like trying to solve a Rubik’s cube while riding a bike. When the elastic holding your shoes upright gives up, you’re in for an interesting game of “catch the spinning shoe”. Mental note: more practice needed!



Photo by Chappell Digital.


The bike course, while not featuring any major climbs, threw 132m of elevation gain at us. I averaged 262W - decent but not my best. Combined with my nutrition oversight and the rising temperature (and my brilliant decision to skip hydration), I was setting myself up for an interesting run.
The flying dismount? Let’s just say my brain sent a very clear “NOPE” signal as I approached the line. Sometimes discretion is the better part of valor, so I opted for a less dramatic stop-and-step approach.
The run started with my legs performing an impromptu cramping routine, followed by a delightful reminder of my recent illness in the form of some very attractive coughing. Between the gravel start (not my favorite), the hills, and my body’s various protests, it wasn’t exactly the strong finish I’d hoped for.
Despite all this, I somehow managed to snag 2nd in my age group - though I’ll admit this says more about the field than my performance-. The winner was in a different league altogether, so hats off to him!



2nd place M40-44. Photo by Chappell Digital.


While this wasn’t my finest showing, it’s important to note that Multisport Canada put on a fantastic event - my struggles were entirely self-inflicted. Looking on the bright side, we now have a baseline for the season. And hey, there’s nowhere to go but up from here… right?

title: Bracebridge Sprint Triathlon
text:
Back racing in Bracebridge after the 2023 Age Group victory. However, defending the title would have not been easy, as a quick look at the people around me in transition was suggesting a much more competitive field than the 2023 race.
I was given the number 22, as opposed to the 120 i had last year. This means I could not get the moral boost of catching people. I mostly had the pressure to not be caught.
The swim felt OK. I opted to swim with the wetsuit (in 2023 I did not use it). It turns out my swim was almost 1m slower this year. It could be because of a stronger current on the second half of the swim, but maybe I just need to get better at swimming with a wetsuit, and to push harder for the 750m of the swim.
In T1 I opted to leave the shoes on the ground, not on the bike. I did this because I struggled with a running mount on my last race, and I knew that the bike leg started uphill, immediately followed by a 90deg corner and a 180 deg corner, leaving little time to fiddle with shoes. So I decided to not put the shoes on the bike, and just do a run dismount into T2. I think it worked out OK.
Then the bike. As always, I felt strong on the bike, and I was catching people up, although I did not know their age group or even if they were racing in the triathlon or the duathlon.
Finally, the run. I knew the run started with a 200 uphill, so I took it easy there. I then went steady, focusing on keeping ~340W, which felt manageable. At around the 3K marker I caught up with a guy that had 43 written on his calf. He was in my age group. I passed him and I heard him trying to stay with me. I was hoping he gave up, because I did not have much more left to react to a defensive move. Luckily, he did not have anything left. He was the guy that ended up 3rd in the age group, about 1m behind me.
At the end I finished in 1h15m54s. About 1.5m faster than last year. of this 90s, about 60came form the bike and 30 came from the run. In the swim I lost time. Both transitions were also faster.
As for the ranking, I could not defend my 2023 title. The guy who finished first, and Australian, was way faster in every discipline. He was about 3min faster on the swim, 2min faster on the bike, and 1m faster on the run. I might be able to get to run at that pace, and with a similarly spech’ed bike I might be able to post the same time, but the swim was just way too fast for me. I really need to find a way to work on my swim if I want to step up the game.

text:
My first triathlon. Organized by the Sheffield Triathlon Club in Hathersage, in the middle of the Peak District. A great place. I do not remember the distances exactly, but they were a bit odd, somewhere in between a sprint and a standard, except for the swim that was a short one in a heated outdoor pool. The main “selling” point was that, has the name implies and because of the venue (the Peak District), it was “hilly”. Very hilly…
I went to this race with my girlfriend. I rented a car that was too small for the job, but somehow I managed to fit the bike in the boot. We got there very early, even before most of the marshals. It was nice to see the calm water of the pool before anyone had the chance to jump in or to set up the lanes.
I set up the bike in T1 and the run kit in T2 (they had different transition zones), double and triple checking I had everything I needed laid out. I then went to the race briefing listening to every world, even if it was the usual obvious stuff (shared roads, dismount line, rack the bike before you take the helmet off, etc.).
When the race started I was quite nervous, not knowing if I had it in me to finish a triathlon race. At the time I did not have a multi-sport watch. I was planning to swim with the Garmin Swim, and then change over to another watch. Except in the excitement of the first race I messed up everything. To this day I am not sure with what piece of tech I finished the race…
Anyway, the swim went as good as it could have: I did not drawn and I finished it. The bike was OK. A challenging route, with plenty of hills and wind, but fun. The real problems started with T2. After I chenged into my running gear, I guess I started to pay my dues to the inexperience. First I could not find the exit to the run. I had to ask my girlfriend where I had to go. Finally, I was out running. But not for long. Very quickly, the run started to feel more like an orienteering race than a triathlon race. The idea was to run up and down into the woods on a hill. Except there was little to no signalling or marshaling. I got lost a couple of time and my watch told me I did almost 1Km more than I was supposed to. It was of little consolation knowing that I was not the only one. I remember seeing people that somehow ended up running on a road well out of the running route…
All in all, it was a good and fun race. I have never done it again because I was not a fun of the hilly run with poor marking, but if that is you jam, go for it, you won’t regret doing the Hathersage Hilly Triathlon.

title: Mixed Team Relay — Wollongong Worlds
text:
If the individual race was the “main event,” the mixed team relay was the fun, social one — yet no less exciting.
For those unfamiliar, a mixed relay team consists of four athletes (woman / man / woman / man), each completing a mini triathlon of about 600 m swim, 6 km bike, and 1.3 km run before tagging the next teammate. It’s fast, intense, and over in less than two hours — pure energy from start to finish.

title: Mixed Team Relay — Wollongong Worlds
text:
Team & Pre-race
Four days before the race, I met my teammates at the Boathouse: Lisa, Irina, and Gregory. Together, we were Team Canada III (X160).



Team at the Boathouse


The day before the race I joined the swim familiarization. The water looked calm and inviting — much easier than the individual event had been. While I was swimming, Lisa picked up our race packs (stickers for arms/calves/bike/helmet, timing chip, team cap, etc.).






Bike prep (the night before)



During the individual race my bike was constantly squeaking and crackling. I tried to isolate it — crankset, cassette, jockey wheels — but with the chain off the bottom bracket was quiet. I had recently switched to a wax-based lube; if it gets contaminated, it can get very noisy. The fix is a deep clean + re-wax. Time was short, so I raced with the noise.


(Future me note: once back home, a proper deep clean plus oil-based lube made it silky smooth. I also replaced slightly bent wheel skewers — possibly part of the problem. Lesson learned: pre-trip bike prep matters.)

title: Mixed Team Relay — Wollongong Worlds
text:
Race Morning
Another relaxed start: we met at 9:00 a.m. at transition to sticker bikes, bags, and ourselves, and set up as usual. Then we moved to the relay holding area — a sequence of gated zones. First, only leg-1 athletes entered; later they opened for leg-2 (me), and so on. Inside, we received the team timing chip and waited. A big screen and a loudspeaker called teams, but they occasionally glitched, so we also scanned the chute ourselves.
I spotted Lisa charging in, we tagged — and I was off.



Ready to check in

title: Mixed Team Relay — Wollongong Worlds
text:
My Leg
Swim (600 m). Slower than I expected despite calm water and low traffic. I went no wetsuit; usually that’s fine for me.
T1 + Bike (6 km). Transition smooth. The course was a shortened version of the individual loop: technical open, a slightly bigger early hill, then fast and flat. The soundtrack: my bike’s full creak orchestra.
T2 + Run (1.3 km). Clean T2. The run mirrored the individual route but counterclockwise and without the big hill, just a descent into the harbour where I tagged Irina for leg 3.
We cheered Irina in, then headed to Lang Park to await Gregory. The leg-4 athletes finished at the main event park — same finish as the individual race.

title: Mixed Team Relay — Wollongong Worlds
text:
Result & Vibes
We placed 21st of 40 teams — solid for an improvised squad with no podium expectations. The real goal was to have fun, and we absolutely did. We wrapped the day watching the elites, sharing a couple of drinks, and taking in the closing ceremony — a brilliant finish to an unforgettable week.

title: Wollongong Worlds: My Overall Experience
text:
“Competing at Worlds wasn’t just a race — it was a celebration of everything that led there.”

Going to the World Championships is one of those moments you can only dream about when you first start in the sport — a distant goal that somehow feels impossible. When the email confirming my qualification arrived, it hit me: this was it. Years of training, early mornings, and determination had led to this.
Representing Canada made it even more meaningful. Wearing the maple leaf among the best age-group athletes from around the world filled me with pride — and a sense of belonging to something bigger than myself.



In the weeks before the trip, excitement mixed with anxiety. Beyond racing, I worried about logistics: would my bike survive the journey? Would my luggage make it? I checked my packing list more times than I’d like to admit.



Goodbye Toronto.


The trip itself was a marathon — over 30 hours of travel and plenty of airport waiting. I refreshed my AirTag app every few minutes to make sure the bike was on the right terminal, waiting to be loaded on the plane. When I finally landed in Sydney around 9 a.m., I learned my room wouldn’t be ready until 3 p.m.



One of the million times I checked the “Find My” app.


So, instead of resting, I dropped my bags and walked straight to the race venue to register and explore the expo. It was hot, I was tired, and all I wanted was a shower — but somehow I ended up walking more than 20,000 steps that day. The adrenaline of finally being there carried me through.
.jpg)




Day 2 started with a short shake-out run and a quick stop to tune up the bike. Then came the Team Canada lunch at the Boathouse — a perfect spot by the water. It was great to finally meet the people I’d only known through emails and group chats, including my mixed relay teammates.



Team Canada.


Later that afternoon, we had swim familiarization, followed by the Parade of Nations in the evening. Another 20,000-step day. All athletes gathered at Flagstaff Hill, standing behind their national flags before walking down to Lang Park.
The ceremony opened with a Land Acknowledgement and a Smoke Ceremony, followed by a live performance of the Australian national anthem.



At the Opening Ceremony in Lang Park.






By Day 3, my body started to protest. My calves felt tight from all the walking, so I spent most of the day in the hotel with my legs up and compression socks on. Later, I checked in my bike — the ritual that makes everything suddenly feel real.



Bike raked.


Day 4 was individual race day. My start time was later in the morning, which gave me a chance to enjoy the buzz around transition and soak in the atmosphere. I’ll save the race details for the next post, but racing on that course — with that crowd and that competition — was every bit as special as I’d imagined.



Individual race done!






The day after the race was all about recovery. I went to the team relay swim familiarization and watched the elites racing the T100 event — yet another victory for Hayden Wilde and a strong show by Kate Waugh.



Swim venue for the mixed team relay.


Day 6 was relay day: fast, intense, and a lot of fun. I’ll share the race details in its own post. For some reason, I thought that we were not allowed to pick up the bikes until 2pm, so after the race I went back to the hotel to shower and eat. When I got back to the venue to watch the elites racing the Standard distance, I realized the transition area was already open. I could have picked up the bike earlier and save a trip back to the hotel…
That evening, I joined some Team Canada athletes for drinks, watched the medal and closing ceremonies, and listened to speeches from the local mayor and triathlon officials. The event ended with the passing of the flag from Wollongong to Pontevedra.



Series winners - the elite men.





Series winners - the elite women.






Day 7 was the long journey back. More airports, more waiting, and more obsessive AirTag tracking to make sure my bike was following along. By the time I finally got home, the week felt like a blur — a mix of exhaustion, pride, and gratitude.



OK, the bike is still with me.


Competing at Worlds wasn’t just about a single race. It was a celebration of everything that led there — the training, the people, the resilience. Wollongong will always be the week where all those years of effort came together in one unforgettable moment. Hopefully there will be more Worlds to come, but you can never forget the first one!



Goodnight Wollongong, it has been an unforgettable experience.

title: 2025 Season Planning
text:
Image generated by DALL-E.


When one season ends, it’s time to take a break—at least a couple of weeks. As the break winds down, I start planning for the next season. In this post, I’ll walk you through my process.

Step 1: Choose the Races
For me, the process always starts with selecting the races I want to tackle in the new season. My usual criteria are pretty subjective—proximity, races I’ve enjoyed before, or ones I’ve never tried. However, this year is a bit different.
Since I qualified for the Age Group World Championship, that race is non-negotiable. From there, I chose races that align with key points in the season where I can gauge my preparation. Another factor I considered was the race course itself. For example, I’m not used to open water swims in the ocean, so I opted for a race in a large body of water to simulate challenging swim conditions.
Here are the races I selected:

Gravenhurst (June 8): The first race of the season. In Canada, races start late, so there aren't many options before this date.
Bracebridge (July 13): A familiar course that provides excellent historical data to measure progress.
Wasaga Beach (August 23): A swim in a large, often windy lake to test my skills in choppy water.
Wollongong (October 17): The World Championship.

I may add one or two smaller races to fine-tune my readiness, but these are the main events.


Step 2: Assign Race Priority
The next step is assigning a priority to each race, from A (high importance) to C (low importance). This step is crucial because your training schedule—including tapering—depends on these priorities. For example, A races require longer tapering phases, while C races may have little to no taper.
Here's how I prioritized my races:

Gravenhurst: C
Bracebridge: B
Wasaga Beach: C
Wollongong: A



Step 3: Define Training Blocks
I'm a big fan of Joe Friel’s periodization system. According to this approach, your training progresses through distinct phases, such as base, build, peak, and taper. Each phase has a specific focus, balancing training volume and intensity while addressing your individual weaknesses.
If you're unfamiliar with this system, check out Joe Friel's blog or his book The Triathlete's Training Bible. The TrainingPeaks blog is another excellent resource.
In the past, I used a mix of DIY tools to plan my season and sessions. While this was effective, it was also incredibly time-consuming. To simplify things, I started using TrainingPeaks, occasionally purchasing pre-made plans. These plans worked well, and the platform’s analytics were top-notch.
But life happens. Illness, work, or other commitments can disrupt even the best-laid plans. Adjusting a pre-made training plan isn’t always easy, and many plans don’t account for changes in your fitness over time. For these reasons, I switched to HumanGo two seasons ago.
HumanGo is an AI-based virtual coach (named Hugo) that adapts your plan based on your performance and availability. Hugo can adjust your schedule if you need to skip sessions or if your fitness improves. While it’s not perfect—AI can occasionally get things wrong—I’ve seen great results. After all, I qualified for the Age Group World Championship using this system.



The 2025 season.


If money were no object, I’d recommend hiring a real-life coach. But for those of us with budget constraints, HumanGo is a fantastic alternative.


Step 4: Trust the Process
Once your plan is set, the key is to trust it. This can be challenging, especially with a new training system. However, it’s crucial to follow the prescribed workouts—even the easy ones! Avoid the temptation to push harder than necessary, as this can lead to injury or burnout.
Monitor your progress, and if you’re not improving after a few months, consider making changes. But start from a place of trust. And remember: consistency is the most important factor in improving. Stay consistent by having fun and staying injury-free (again, don’t race your easy workouts!).
Good luck with your planning, and here’s to a successful 2025 season!

title: Welcome To My Blog
text:
The first race: Heathersage Hilly Triathlon, UK, 2013


Welcome!
I’m a 40-year-old amateur triathlete with a passion for swimming, cycling, and running. By day, I navigate the corporate world in a 9-to-5 office job, but my heart truly comes alive when I’m training for my next race.
Let’s start with some introduction.

Planting the triathlon seed
My triathlon journey started in 2000 while watching the Summer Olympics—the first time triathlon was included in the schedule. I remember thinking how incredible those athletes were, swimming, then cycling, and then running. It seemed impossible, especially since I couldn’t even swim.
Fast forward to 2012. I was living in Yorkshire, England, where the sport was impossible to ignore, especially with the Brownlee brothers dominating the international scene.
At that time, I had started participating in some casual running races. Nothing major, but it was a start.
Then fate stepped in—someone stole my motorbike. Instead of replacing it, I decided to buy a road bike.


Race on!
That’s when I decided to give triathlon a shot. I signed up for a local event with a short, pool-based swim and began training. I followed a pre-packaged Garmin plan while learning to swim from scratch.
I somehow made it to the starting line and, miraculously, to the finish line too. I made every rookie mistake possible: sprinting too hard in the swim and gasping for air after 50m, losing my bike in transition, getting lost on the run course, fumbling with my watch…
But none of that mattered. I fell in love with the sport and wanted more.


Today
Fast forward to 2024—while much remains the same, everything has also changed. I still love the sport, but I’m now more experienced in my training, albeit older and slower. Between my 9-to-5 job, wife, and two kids, triathlon isn’t my only commitment. I have other hobbies that demand attention too. Balancing everything is a delicate art.
Follow this blog to join me on my racing journey and see how I manage this balancing act.

title: 2025: Destination Wollongong!
text:
I’m writing this post a few months after the dust has settled. Back in early 2024, I set a big goal for myself: qualify for the Age Group World Championship for Sprint Triathlon. This decision was fueled partly by the ego boost of winning the Bracebridge race last year (let’s be honest, who doesn’t love a little ego boost?). On top of that, I dug into the winning times from qualifying races over the past 3–4 years. While I wasn’t quite there yet, I figured that with a bit of luck—and maybe some roll-down magic—I might just make it happen.
For those unfamiliar, the qualification process in Canada is straightforward on paper but gets tricky when you try to explain it. Let me try anyway.
First, the basics. To qualify, you need to:
- Be a Canadian citizen or permanent resident.
- Have a valid Canada Triathlon membership.
- Race in one of the Canadian qualifying events (technically, you can qualify abroad, but that’s a tougher route).
- Express your interest by filling out a form and paying a small fee a few days before the race.
With those boxes ticked, you’re off to the races. Now, winning the event is obviously great, but it’s not always necessary—or even a guarantee of qualification. Why? Because what really matters is your federation ranking, not the event ranking. And here’s where things get a little funky:

Who’s really in the race?
You might not win your event, but if the people who beat you aren’t racing to qualify—or aren’t eligible—they don’t count in the federation ranking.
Age shuffling madness.
The federation ranking is based on the next calendar year’s world championship. So, while the event uses your age as of 2024, the federation looks at your age as of 2025. This means people might move up to the next age group, which can reshuffle the rankings in surprising ways.

Basically, if you want to be absolutely sure you’ve qualified, you need to be the fastest in both your age group and the one below it. No pressure, right?
Oh, and did I mention that in Ontario, we have only three qualifying races, with just one slot per age group at each? Simple to understand? Maybe. Simple to explain? Not so much.
Now, back to my 2024 season. The three qualifying events were Guelph, Welland, and Barrie. Things didn’t start great—I finished 5\(^{th}\) in both Guelph and Barrie. Welland went better, where I snagged 2\(^{nd}\) place, but two younger athletes also posted faster times. So, I had three people ahead of me, leaving my qualification chances looking slim.
By September 11\(^{th}\), I still hadn’t heard from the federation and assumed it wasn’t happening. I’d already started planning a more laid-back 2025, given how demanding this season had been. After dinner, I was casually cleaning out my spam inbox (as one does), and there it was—a message from the federation: I got a direct qualification spot!
Cue panic. I had until September 13\(^{th}\) to confirm, and apparently, I’d missed earlier emails that also ended up in spam. A quick chat with my wife followed—this was an expensive and poorly-timed opportunity, but how often do you get the chance to represent your adoptive country on the world stage? We decided it was worth it.
So, Wollongong, here I come!

Looking at those point totals now – 90 (Welland), 90 (Bracebridge), and 75 (Barrie) – each number represents a story, a race where I pushed my limits and competed against not just others, but myself. title: 2025 Season Recap: A World Championship Season
text:
Every triathlon season tells a story — not just of watts, splits, and meters swum, but of consistency, learning, and the daily choices that shape the big picture.
Between October 2024 and October 2025, I logged roughly 380 hours of structured training across swim, bike, run, and strength work. The load was significantly higher than last year and comparable to 2023.
In this post, I’ll cover both the metrics and the meaning behind them: monthly training trends, load distribution, and how key markers like FTP, pace, and heart rate changed through the season. But more importantly, I’ll share what those numbers meant — the highs that built confidence, the lows that tested patience, and how it all came together -or not- on race day.

title: 2025 Season Recap: A World Championship Season
text:
Monthly Distribution
I like to look at monthly training time to assess consistency. Ideally, volume remains fairly stable, with a gentle decline during race season as intensity ramps up.
 
I built volume steadily from October 2024 through January 2025, followed by a dip in February (I caught a cold then). The biggest drop came between April and July — partly due to racing, partly to a motivation dip, and critically, to growing doubts about the Humango coaching platform I was using at the time. Things normalized again after July.

title: 2025 Season Recap: A World Championship Season
text:
Performance Chart
Training volume is only part of the story. To track fitness, I rely on the TRIMP curve in Golden Cheetah — a metric similar to TrainingPeaks’ TSS, combining intensity and duration.



Yearly TRIMP score. The TRIMP score is in solid blue, the load in pink, and the fatigue in green.


As expected from the mid-season dip, TRIMP dropped in those months. On the bright side, fitness peaked right before my A race at Worlds, with fatigue well under control (around -4 the day before the individual race). Though race-week logistics certainly added some hidden fatigue, the numbers suggest I timed the peak well.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
Finis Smart Swim Goggles
I have been using the Finis Smart Goggles for a bit over a week. This is a first impressions review. If something significant will come up, I’ll keep you posted.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
News
The first tab is the “News” tab. Here you’ll find an overview of your latest swim, notifications from the community, if you’ve added any friend to the app, and a look at your achievements.



News tab


We’ll look at a swim analysis later. I do not have any friend connected to my profile, so I cannot show you that one, but here is how the Achievements looks like.



Achievements


These are a bit like the Garmin’s Badges. You do not set them up, you just get achievements as you go.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
History



Swim history


Here you just see a list of your swims and how you track against swim goals that you set yourself. The workout listed can be filtered, but for now the filtering is fairly limited: You can only search for workouts that you tagged as “favourites”.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
Pool
Here you can register your pools. The main use is to make sure you set the pool length correctly, but if you like to know how much you swim at different pools, you can use satisfy your curiosity here.



Pools

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
Settings
When it comes to settings, there is a limited but adequate numbers of things you can change. We saw already you can register a pool. Of course, you can then tell the goggles which pool you will be swimming in. Other settings include the appearance of the screen and the fields you see when you swim. Let’s have a look.



Main settings screen



Screen adjustments



Screen adjustments


You can change two things: the screen brightness and the writing position. Being able to change the writing position can help you if you find that the screen is a bit too much far off the left.
As for the demo mode, I am not sure what it does since when I tried to toggle it I did not really see anything happening, but I guess it is nothing important.


Screen fields



Swim screen fields


This part is a bit confusing. You can choose between 4 different preset:

Standard swim
I swim laps
I swim for times
I swim sets
I swim stroke sets

Each preset will show you three fields, which will alternate between when you turn, when you rest, and when you are actually swimming. What makes it challenging is that many fields are shared between the presets, making for very small different differences between them. On top of that, it is not very clear what each option actually mean until you try it. For example, is the timer a lap timer, or a set timer? You will need to go for a swim and find out.
To simplify, I think that most triathlete will use two presets:

Standard swim or I swim laps (they are virtually identical) for pool swims.
I swim for time for open water swims.

In essence, with these settings you will see:

Lap swim time
Set swim time
A lap counter for the set
Rest time
Total swim time

Interestingly, the goggles will never show you the pace, even if they know the lap time and the pool length. So a bit of math is required. If you target 1:40min/100m and you swim a 25m pools, you will need to clock 25s/lap.
Finally, you will see that there is a toggle to enable “short hand display”. If you like to make the UI more confusing, that option will remove all English writing, so instead of seeing “Clock 5:40” you will see “5:40”. You will just need to guess/remember if what you are looking at is rest time, clock time, swim time, set time…

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
3D Video analysis
A feature that sets the Finis goggles apart from other offerings is the 3D video analysis. Naturally the goggles track your head position for the whole swim, that’s how they know if you are swimming, resting, turning, etc. But Finis takes this data a step further. They use it to reconstruct a 3D video of your head movements for the entire length of the swim.
You can interact with the video and rotate it as much as you like, and you can see things like how still you head is, if you move too much to the left or to the right when you breath, if you keep it level or if you “look up” too much, etc.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
The good
Those goggles have a lot to go for them. They are cheaper than the competition. They are modular, so you can simply replace the goggles, and not the whole thing. They are accurate. In all my swims they have not under- or over- counted laps once, and they never failed to detect a swim set as opposed to a kick set. Some other reviewers criticized that the screen is way to off to the left and you have to make an effort to see it, but I find that it is not that bad, and I like that if I do not want to see my metric, I can just ignore the screen.
The app is simple, but it offers enough functionality, and it syncs without issues with the goggles. Finally, the 3D video is a nice feature.

title: New kit: Finis Swim Smart goggles
text:
What can be improved
For as much as I like them, the goggles are not perfect. To start with, I wish that the button was a bit easier to press. But maybe it will jest get a bit softer with time.
Then there is the data displayed itself. It works, but I would like if it was better documented. Also, I would love to see the pace displayed as well as just timers.
I said earlier that I like the 3D video. And it is true it is a really neat feature. However, it does feel half baked. I think it would be much more powerful if they could give you some feedback. I think that combining this with some AI analysis would enhance the experience, although I am afraid that will also open the doors to a subscription model.
I have not used the goggles in open water yet (March in Canada…), but I will let you know if anything drastically different comes up. However, I do know that I would like to see the addition of a GPS chipset to give pace feedback in open water. Easier said than down, as GPS signal does not work underwater, and your face is underwater most of the time while you swim. Other companies have enabled a sync with GSP watches to provide the functionality.
Another open water feature that is missing but present in the Form goggles is the “swim straight” feature. This features helps you swim in. straight line in open water, and it does not require GPS. However, it will be challenging to implement in the Finis goggles as they do not have a HUD always displayed in front of you, but a smaller one tucked away on the side.
The final criticism I have for the Finis is their limited third party sync support. They can only share data with Strava, Swim.com, and Apple Healthkit. For now, this works for me since I still wear my watch anyway while I swim, but otherwise not being able to directly load my data to TrainingPeaks or Humango would be a major pain point. Hopefully they will expand their partnerships in the future. At the very least, being able to download the raw .fit file would allow to re-upload it to any other platform.

title: S. Bertilla Boscardin - Torneo Di Basket
text:
Here I was in my element: a basketball tournament. This was organized by my high-school, and each class was competing against the each other. It was a complete obliteration of the competition. there were not really many other guys used to play at the level I was playing at the time, and even then I could count on another super strong girl in my class. At the end, we just destroyed everyone. It almost wasn’t even fun at then end. Almost…
I particularly remember two matches.
In one, we came close to a brawl. I stole the ball and sprinted away for a solo counterattack, when somebody from the other team decided to just push me on the floor. Memories flushed before my eyes, as that is exactly how I broke one elbow a few years prior. This time, there was no injury, but I sprang up looking for the guy. Luckily he was quick to apologize and it ended there. And I say luckily for myself as well, as he was a bit bigger than me, and I have no experience at all being in a fight, so I don’t think getting into one would have been a great idea anyway.
The other match I remember well was a strange one. It was against the class of a guy I was playing against in the provincial teams tournament, and his specialty was 3 points shoots. I have never been a good long range shooter. I have always got out of trouble getting into the paint. The match started with him ding what he was good at, scoring every single long distance shot he was taking. And here is the strange thing. A couple of times I was completely open on the 3 points line, and I took the shot. And I made it. That must have gave me confidence or something, and I started to shoot more and more, and scoring more and more. It ended up almost looking like a 2024 NBA match: a 3 points contest, rather than a basketball game. But that time it worked for us, as we won the match.

title: 3 Port Tour
text:
This was a tough one. I prepared for it by progressively hitting 100K to 120K rides, but 160K is something different.
The route was very flat, except for two short but brutal uphill. I started off on my own, and around the 40K marker I caught a small group. We took turns in front, but it was a bit of a mistake. That made me push a bit too hard too early.
At around 100K there was a lunch break. The stands were very well stocked with plenty of options. Past, pizza, fruit, etc. I was not planning to stop for long, so I was mostly worried about avoiding getting my legs to seize up, and overeating. I did not overeat, in hindsight, I should have another serving of pasta.
A bit after lunch there was the worst part. A long stretch of road on the sun, no shade, slightly uphill. That cooked me good.
The last 20K or so were also pretty hard, between the heath and the accumulated tiredness, it was hard to bring the bike home.
But I did. Overall a fun day out, even if not my favourite kind of sporting challenge. The only major downside is that cycling events like this are more like a parkrun that a competition. There is plenty of time to chat, but no official timing, ranking, or medal.

title: Milton Subaru Triathlon
text:
This was a wet one. It rained all the time. Before the race, during, and after. Everything got drenched (pro tip: bring a change to leave in the car, so that it stays dry).
This was a race done in preparation of the qualifying ones I will be doing later in the year. The distance was a bit odd (30K bike, 7.5K run), halfway between a sprint and a standard.
I did a course rec a week before the race, and I knew there was a long and pretty steep raod. That will be interesting to do with wet conditions.
My main concern going in was the water temperature. Luckily, the water was perfect. Around 20C. It was a mass start, but a civilized one, so not much fighting at all.
I just kept telling myself to swim relaxed, don’t go in the red. And I did come out of the water feeling quite good, maybe too good for a race, but still I swam at 1:46/100m, which is better than any other swim race I have ever done.
The the bike leg started. The first issue was that I decided to try to keep my shoes attached to the bike this time, but I did not use elastic bands to secure them horizontally. Putting the shoes one while riding was challenging, because they were constantly rotating the wrong way around. Next time, I’ll use elastics. From there, it was again a matter of managing effort. Knowing the challenging course profile and that this was a longer race than a sprint triathlon, I just gauged the effort.
I was surprised by the grip my Continental tires have. Not a single time on the bike course I felt like the bike could send me off.
Finally, the run. My legs were not into it at all, and the few hills along the course did not helped. On top of it, a portion of about 2.5K was turned into a mud fest by the rain. Not my preferred running conditions. It was not an horrible run looking at the clock, but for sure it was not a pleasant one.
Also, turns out that my fancy carbon plated running shoes can give me blisters wif my feet are wet and there is grit inside the shoes. Not great.

title: Welland Rose City Sprint Triathlon
text:
Another qualifying event. On paper, the route profile for the bike and the run were much easier than Guelph. An almost flat course.
The swim was in a canal used for boat racing. I only learnt about this after the race, but something to keep in mind for the next time: the long sides were following the race buoy guides. So, to swim the shortest route possible, just follow the submerged guides. Like swimming in a pool.
As I said, I did not know that. I managed to swim fairly straight with a GPS swim distance of 780m, so 30m more than the official distance. At a 2min/100m pace, this would have cost me roughly 25s. We will come back to this later.
It was an odd swim. It was swimsuit optional, but for those trying to qualify swimsuits were not allowed. As a result, there was a mixed field of people with and without wetsuit, make it a bit unfair. Also, for those qualifying, the “non westuit” policy will be enforced on a honorary base…
Anyway, I my swim felt OK. I was controlling my breathing better than in Guelph, and it felt like the water was moving fast next to me. Except, when I got of the water and looked at my watch, I saw a swim time of 17min. WTF! How did that happen?!?
But it was no time to think about it. A short run to T1, and off for the bike leg. And here I had a small problem with the pedals. I did attach my shoes with elastics, but the elastics came off too soon, and the shoes did not want to stay up straight. To put them on I had to stop, take them off the pedal, put them on, and start cycling again. It felt like an eternity.
Then the reality of the bike course hit. It was flat, yes, but very windy. Every second half of each of the 5 laps felt like going uphill. I was catching up a lot of people, but when I was looking at the fast looking guys as a reference it did not look like I was gaining anything on them. Truth be told, most of them were probably under 30, but still…
Finally, on the run. The route was flat, but made slow but a few sharp corners. And as always, my legs refused to collaborate. In fairness, probably I did push a bit too much on the bike. In places, my watch was telling I was going as slow as 5:05min/Km.
Total race time: 1h18m. My slowest sprint triathlon ever.
After some time, I decided to look at the results online. 2nd on the age group! I guess it was a tough race for everyone. And also a reminder to not compare triathlon races with each other: each race is completely different.
So that was good. The annoying bit was that I finished 22s behind the first. So close to having a chance to qualify. Makes me wonder what if I swam closer to the 750m? Or what if I did a better T1? Or I pushed just a bit more on the run? Too late know, cannot win races with “what ifs.
The last annoying bit of the day was the very long delay for the award: almost 3h between the end of the race and the awards ceremony. An eternity.
But I made a friend: the guy who finished 3rd: Robert Eso. We’ll meet again later this year in Berrie.

title: Barrie Sprint Triathlon
text:
This was the last qualifying event of the season. It was an early start. To be in Barrie at 6am, I left at 4am from Burlington.
It was a cold morning. So cold that the water temperature went was down to 16C from the 20C of the day before, and with the water that cold it was a westsuit mandatory race. A few people did not have wetsuit, and they got moved to the duathlon race. This probably messed up the results (more on this later).
Rob Eso, the guy I met in Welland (he finished third), was there too. So one of my main objective was to finish ahead of him.
I was not feeling 100%, but I started off reasonably well. I closed the swim in just over 14min. Nothing incredible, but pretty decent for me.
I got to transition and I could not see Rob’s bike. I though he must have out swam me, which in fairness is a fairly easy thing to do.
T1 was not great, as with cold feet and cold hands it was a struggle to get the wetsuit off. Once again, I opted to put the shoes on, and not leave them on the bike, which worked out OK.
Off to the bike leg. 4 laps on very fast and very fast tarmac. I probably did not push out enough watts, but I still kept an average speed of about 37km/h. I was seeing Rob on some the straight, and I noticed I was catching up, but not fast enough. Damn! I though, he must have had a killer swim to be so much ahead.
Then we got to T2. Again I did not see Rob’s bike there, which I found really strange. But off to run I went. As always, I did not feel fast at all, but it turned out to be a 22min run, which is in line with all the other runs of the season. During the straights, I saw Rob again, He was surprisingly behind, and he looked like he was not going particularly fast.
And finally, the finish line.
I checked the results: 5\(^{th}\) in the Age Group. A bit disappointing, since a 5\(^{th}\) place is not going to give a spot, but I need to remember that I cannot control who shows up the races, only what I do. And clearly in this race there were a lot of strong people.
But back to the mess of the timing for a second. Many official records, including mine, are incomplete, mostly missing the bike leg. For example, my record has a 14min swim, no bike, and a 53min run. Clearly, the run includes the bike leg as well.
The official records also say I finished 6\(^{th}\), not 5\(^{th}\). But when I look at the results of the guy who finished first, they are just not believable for a sprint triathlon from a 40-ish years old. First of all, the total time was 1h1min. Which would be a time that can compete with a 25 years old pro. Second, he also was missing the bike record, but his swim leg was 20min, and his run leg was 40min. Now, if you swim in 20min, you are unlikely fit enough to do a 20K bike and a 5K run in 40min. On top of that, 40min for a 20K bike and a 5K run would be an insanely fast split for an amateur 40-ish years old triathlete. Personally, I believe he did a duathlon instead. In that case, the first 20min would be for the 5K run, and the remaining 40min for the 20K bike and the 2.5K run, which is reasonable.
Finally, back to Rob. Turns out he swam in 15min, so I won there, then he cycled at 36km/h (again, point for me), but he messed up because he did 5 laps instead of 4. That took some wind out of his sail and finished the run in 23min. That sucks. I did that mistake in Birmingham years ago, and I know it is infuriating.

title: Indoor Triathlon Provincial Championship Series - Race 1
text:
Scoring
The scoring was simple:

Swim: 10 points per 25m
Bike: 25 points per 500m
Run: 25 points per 200m (or 13 points per 100m on the last lap)

Competitors were ranked in 10-year age groups, but only the overall ranking counted for the Indoor Provincial Championship.
Now, let’s rewind to where it all began.
The race took place at Toronto Pan Am, a venue that hosts international-level competitions. Going from my local Brampton pool to this place? Yeah, it felt like I had been called up to the big leagues.

title: Bracebridge Sprint Triathlon
text:
M40-45 podium.
Bracebridge, Year Three: When the Race Says “Not Today”
Well, here we are again — back in beautiful Bracebridge for the third year running! This time it’s part of my lead-up to the Age Group World Championships. While this wasn’t meant to be an “A” race, I still showed up hoping to match — or beat — my performances from the last two years.
Spoiler alert: that didn’t happen.

title: Bracebridge Sprint Triathlon
section: The build up to the race
text:
The build up to the race
Let’s rewind a bit. Two weeks out from the race, things started going sideways. Sleep? Barely. I was averaging 5–6 hours a night, never more than two hours in a row. Basically, I was sleepwalking to the start line.
Then the shoulder saga began. I did a 2,600m open water swim in Kennisis Lake and — boom — right shoulder pain. Bad enough that I had to stay out of the water for a week. And when I did get back in, every single open water swim was painfully slower — like 15–20 seconds per 100m slower than my pool pace. Sure, pools are faster (thanks, flip turns), but that kind of drop? Come on.
As if that wasn’t enough, my wetsuit felt like it was trying to suffocate me. I might’ve gained a bit of muscle lately (thanks, strength training!), and the suit just wasn’t having it. It even gave me a couple of cuts near the shoulders, and I could feel water rushing into the sleeves. If wetsuits ended up being optional, I was 100% ditching it.
Oh, and I did something really smart too — went kayaking for 30+ km over a few days at the cottage, just because I love it. My shoulder had just recovered and I figured, “Why not?” Turns out: because you have a race coming up is why not.

title: Bracebridge Sprint Triathlon
text:
Race day. Let’s go.

Swim



Swim.


My swim strategy was “don’t blow up.” I stayed calm, maybe too calm. In hindsight, I think I could’ve gone faster even if I went into the red. My time? Over 17 minutes for 750m — easily one of my slowest swims ever. Not exactly the tone I wanted to set.


T1
T1 was smooth — until the end. I made the ultimate rookie mistake: unracked the bike before putting my helmet on. Yep. That rule you literally can’t miss because your helmet is on the handlebars? Broke it. A referee saw me, said something ending in “5-second penalty” (should’ve been 15?), but didn’t point me to a penalty box. I never saw one either. So I just… kept going. Not ideal.


Bike



Bike.


Onto the bike. This is usually where I claw back some ground. Not today. Everyone around me had slick TT bikes and looked strong. I had my road bike, and recently removed the aero bars, so I was still adjusting to the new position. Oh, and my Garmin decided to nap through the whole ride — wouldn’t start, wouldn’t record, wouldn’t even pretend to work. I tried to fire up a new activity mid-race but gave up. So, I rode blind.
And just when I thought things couldn’t get worse, twice I got stuck behind confused drivers on course who slowed me down to a crawl. Final time: 39:12 for 20k — that’s just over 30.6 km/h. Ouch. More than 2 minutes slower than my first year here. No power, no data, no juice.


T2
T2? Fine. I didn’t trust my flying dismount, so I played it safe and stepped off. No drama. Still no sign of a penalty marker, so I just kept going.


Run



Run.


The run. Oh boy. Let’s call it what it was: a shuffle. One of my slowest 5ks ever at 24:12 — 2 minutes off last year’s pace. It was 30°C by then, which didn’t help, but honestly? I just didn’t have the legs or the fire. My body was like, “Hard pass.”

title: Bracebridge Sprint Triathlon
text:
Recap
Final time: 1:22:19. Somehow, that was good enough for 3rd in my age group, which probably says more about the field than my performance. I stuck around for the award ceremony, constantly glancing over my shoulder wondering if I was going to get hit with a disqualification for that helmet snafu.
All in all? Pretty rough day out. But also a much-needed wake-up call. Here’s what I’m taking away from this:

Dial back the fatigue. I think I was carrying too much neuromuscular load and wasn’t prepped for race-level intensity.
More 5K practice. I’ll hit up a few Parkruns to find my legs again.
Recheck my zones. I suspect my Humango high-intensity sessions aren’t quite hitting the right level — or lasting long enough.
New wetsuit. The current one’s officially fired.
Push harder in the water. I need to get used to real effort in open water without falling apart.
More race-specific bricks. Because nothing prepares you for race day like simulating race day.
Prioritize recovery. Like actually. Not just foam rolling and pretending that’s enough.

Next up: Wasaga Beach in a bit over a month. With any luck — and a little smarter prep — I’ll be back on track.
Stay tuned, and if you’ve ever unracked your bike before putting your helmet on… well, at least I’m not alone.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Wasaga Beach is famous for being the longest freshwater sand beach in the world, and it makes for a beautiful triathlon backdrop. This race, organized by Multisport Canada, had an impressive turnout: around 450 participants, nearly double the size of the local races I usually do.
Thankfully, the familiar lineup of vendors was there too—because, yet again, I forgot my race belt. At this point, I really just need to leave one permanently in my tri-bag.
Preparation-wise, I came into this event at the tail end of a solid training block—maybe too solid. Three weeks ago, I ran my fastest 5K in years, and I’d been hitting strong sessions on both the bike and run (even off the bike in brick workouts). But as I’d soon find out, racing doesn’t always follow the script.
Warm-up felt good, and heading into the start I was confident. I knew winning the age group was a long shot with Hector Palacios on the line (he’s seriously fast), and as always, plenty of competitors were on TT bikes, which makes it tough to keep up on a road bike. But before thinking about that, there was the swim.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Swim
The swim was a small-wave mass start in calm, clear water with a straightforward out-and-back course. Perfect conditions—almost.
The catch: a long wade through knee-deep water both into and out of the swim. That’s not something I’m used to, and it turned out to matter more than expected.
I swam conservatively (as always) but a touch faster than in recent races, averaging 1:52/100m instead of my usual >2:00/100m. But as soon as I stood up to run out of the water, both calves and hamstrings seized in sharp cramps. I couldn’t run into transition—I had to walk. That was the start of the day’s unraveling.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Transition Troubles (Again)
When I finally got to the bike, I at least avoided repeating my Bracebridge mistake (touching the bike before putting on the helmet). Helmet first—check.
But the transition gods weren’t done with me. My race belt had gone missing. I usually leave it inside my helmet, under my sunglasses, but it wasn’t there. After nearly a minute of searching, I found it under the bike. With oxygen-deprived race brain, even that simple task felt like a puzzle. Finally, belt on, and off onto the bike.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Bike
The bike course was almost perfectly flat, with a slight downhill bias on the way back. Road surface wasn’t the best—lots of cracks and potholes, but nothing unrideable.
I kept the effort under control, holding back from my usual push partly to avoid re-triggering the cramps and partly to preserve something for the run. Power numbers were solid but not spectacular.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Run
Transition two went smoothly, but the run just wasn’t there. I had hoped to hold 4:20/km pace, but despite my heart rate spiking, the legs refused to respond.
The flat course had a few “obstacles”—patches of sand on the path, a couple short steps and sandy slopes—that normally wouldn’t faze me. But in this state, each one broke rhythm and made it harder to recover. The cramps never fully left; they lingered like a shadow, limiting my stride.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Post-Race Debrief
I crossed the line in 1h16m, finishing 5th in my age group. Respectable on paper, but far from the performance I know I’m capable of. With less than two months to go until the World Championship, it’s frustrating not to have put together a strong race this season.
I’ve had excuses—being sick in one race, now cramps in this one—but at the end of the day, the results aren’t where I want them. Confidence isn’t built on training numbers alone; it needs race execution.
Later that day, I debriefed with my new coach (more on him soon). His feedback was blunt but valuable.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Coach Feedback
Training week issues
- Pacing discipline: I overshoot intervals in over/under workouts, creating unnecessary fatigue.
- Brick sessions: I went too hard, especially on the bike, which left me carrying fatigue into race day.
Race-specific issues
- Cramps were the primary limiter. These are common in cold water (19–22°C) swims with tight wetsuits and long plantarflexion (pointed toes).
- Standing up too suddenly post-swim likely triggered them.
- Bike HR drifted higher than expected, suggesting swim stress + cramp fatigue.
- On the run, cramps disrupted stride mechanics despite a relatively high HR—clearly neuromuscular, not aerobic, limitation.
Cramps were multi-factorial:
- Cold water + wetsuit compression.
- Sudden transition from horizontal to vertical.
- Possibly hydration/electrolytes (though less likely this early).
- Entering the race with cumulative fatigue from double days.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Advice for Next Race

Swim → Bike Transition

Warm-up with calf raises + hamstring curls.

Adjust wetsuit fit so calves/hamstrings aren’t overly compressed.

Stand up gradually, flex ankles before jogging.

Bike Execution

First 2–3 minutes: 200–220W to settle HR.

Then steady 240–260W, capped at ~285–290W on surges.

Keep overall average near 270W without overcooking the legs.

Fuel & Hydration

Bike: 1 gel (~20–25g carbs) + 200–300ml sports drink.

Run: optional sip of water at aid station.

Run Execution

Open the first 500m at 4:35–4:40/km before building.

Aim for 4:25–4:30/km if legs allow.

Use cadence focus (180–182 spm) instead of “push harder” when the legs feel heavy.

title: Wasaga Beach Sprint Triathlon
text:
Final Thoughts
Not the race I wanted, but a good reminder that training fitness doesn’t always translate directly to race-day performance. Small details—like cramp prevention, pacing discipline, and nutrition—can decide whether the legs show up when it matters.
I’m taking these lessons forward into the final block before Worlds. There’s work to do, but better to learn these lessons now than on the biggest stage.

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
For years I had dreamed of this moment — racing at the World Championships, wearing the maple leaf on my suit.
Months and years of structured training, long hours, early mornings — everything led to this.
I reached the start line with excitement, pride… and a bit of fatigue. The travel, the walking around Wollongong, and all the pre-race logistics had taken their toll. Still, the adrenaline of being here overpowered everything else.

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🎒 The Days Before
I collected my race pack the very first day: arm and calf stickers, swim cap, bike and helmet numbers, a transition bag, a nice backpack, a beach towel, and a Welcome to Wollongong booklet.
The next day, I dropped off my bike for the mandatory pre-race check — with 1,260 athletes in the sprint alone, this keeps things organized.
On the way there, I got my first omen: the bike squeaked and cracked with every pedal stroke. Not ideal.



In this races you have to rack the bike the day befre the race. So many bikes!

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
☀️ Race Morning
For once, I didn’t have to wake up at 4 a.m. My start was at 10:45, pure luxury.
I had a calm breakfast, applied my number stickers, and walked to transition.
There, surrounded by incredibly fit athletes from all over the world, it was easy to feel out of place. I reminded myself to stick to my plan and not get distracted.
My setup was dialed in: bike shoes clipped and held by elastics, helmet with sunglasses on the bars, running shoes with a gel tucked inside, race belt ready, and Vaseline around the shoe entry for a fast slip-in.
After some dynamic stretching and elastic-band warm-up, I dropped my bag and headed toward the swim start.

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🏊 Swim — Chaos in the Harbour
A surprise awaited us: due to high waves, the course was moved inside the harbour. For a weaker swimmer like me, that was a relief.
I warmed up briefly in the water, then lined up with my wave — 76 athletes, shoulder to shoulder.
The speaker’s words echoed: “Athletes, you are now in the hands of the starter.”
Heartbeats. Silence. The horn blasted.
Chaos. Bodies everywhere. Some swimmers veered off course, making it hard to stay straight.
I kept calm, knowing that going too hard early would only lead to fading later.
I exited the water 56th of 76 — far from the front, but I wasn’t last, and more importantly, I made the cutoff I had been worried about.



Swim done!

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🚴 Bike — Two Loops of Noise
Transition was long — nearly 400 m from swim exit to bike mount — but it went smoothly for once.
The bike course had two loops: a technical first half with small hills, then a flat, fast stretch back. Perfect variety.
I tried to stay with a group early on, but when they pushed the pace, I let them go.
I didn’t want to repeat past mistakes of blowing up before the run.
I settled around 249 W, slightly below my 255 W goal, but steady.
The only problem: my bike sounded like it was falling apart — constant squeaks and cracks.
I prayed it would hold together to the end.



Bike leg.

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🏃 Run — Holding It Together
T2 was quick, no drama.
My legs felt heavier than I hoped, but I focused on rhythm.
The run course had rolling hills and heat, and I maintained a 4:30 min/km pace — not spectacular, but consistent.
I even managed to pick it up in the last 500 m.
Then came the blue carpet — that magical final stretch.
Crossing the finish arch with a World Championship medal around my neck was a moment I’ll never forget.
