title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🇨🇦 Little Rivalries
I had two “rivals” in mind:
- A Canadian I met at swim familiarization — confident and strong in the water. I ended up beating him.
- Another Canadian from the bike group that had dropped me. I reeled him in on the run and passed him in the final lap, finishing about 10 seconds ahead.
Two small, personal wins that made the day even sweeter.

title: World Championships: The Race of a Lifetime
text:
🏁 Results and Reflections
I finished 56th of 77. Not spectacular on paper, but in context — this was the world’s best amateur field, every athlete here having earned their spot.
My time of 1:15:35 was solid, even a bit faster than my season average given the heat and course difficulty.
I also finished 2nd of 6 Canadians — a proud result.
Looking back at my goals:

Top 10% → not met, but a poor metric anyway since it depends on who shows up.

Time goal (1:10–1:20) → met halfway at 1:15:35.

Don’t fade on the run → ✅

Not last → ✅

Top 3 Canadians → ✅

Most importantly, I executed my plan.
I raced smart, steady, and left the finish line with a smile instead of a grimace.
That, to me, is a success.

text:
MultiSport Canada Champions plaque.
Back-to-back.
After winning the title in 2024, I managed to defend it in 2025 as well. Last year’s win felt like a surprise when I first learned I had topped the series; this time I understood the stakes a little better, which somehow made it both more satisfying and more stressful. If you want the origin story, the first title is in 2024 MultiSport Canada Series Champion!.

I finished on 250 points from three races, which was enough to take the category again. But the part that stands out most is how tight it was underneath. Hector Palacios and Nicholas Yardley both finished on 200 points from only two races.
That is what makes the three-race eligibility rule bittersweet. On one hand, I understand the logic: a series title should reward a full season, not just one or two standout results. From the organizer’s point of view, the structure also makes complete sense. MultiSport Canada is a business, and races only happen if people keep signing up, so of course the series is designed to reward participation and give athletes a reason to come back more often. If you want to win the title, you need to race with them more. On the other hand, it can still feel a little like a pay-to-win system, because participation matters almost as much as raw performance. The gap from first to second was only 50 points. Under this scoring table, that means one additional 10th-place finish would have been enough to erase it, and either of those athletes looked more than capable of doing much better than 10th.
I still take a lot of pride in winning it. A title is a title, and defending one is even harder than winning the first time. But the final table also shows how much these series standings depend on being able to line up often enough across the year.

title: Meadowvale Parkrun
text:
Race Overview
This was not originally on the plan.
Three weeks after my previous Meadowvale parkrun, I was back on the same course for a more practical reason than a race target. I had switched my running power source from the Garmin FR965 built-in estimate to a Stryd footpod, and I needed a hard 5K effort to recalibrate my running power zones.
That made the event useful, but it did not make me feel especially ready for it. I did not feel particularly springy, and my stomach was a little unsettled before the start. During the warm-up I also noticed that my heart rate was rising more easily than I would have liked. None of that was dramatic enough to call the run off, but it was enough to make me think this might be more of a calibration exercise than a performance day.


Before the Start
While scanning the field before the start, I noticed a couple of young girls wearing Toronto cross-country championship T-shirts. That is usually a decent warning sign. I also spotted one or two men who looked like they might be quicker than me.
So the rough expectation was simple: run hard, collect useful power data, and see where that left me. I was not expecting anything spectacular.


How It Went
After the start, one of the two girls I had noticed and one of the quicker-looking men immediately went to the front. Then another guy came flying through from behind at a pace that looked ambitious. He was breathing hard almost straight away, though, and I was ready to bet that he would not be able to hold it.
Spoiler alert: he could not.
Once the early sorting-out was done, the race became fairly uneventful. The girl at the front held the lead comfortably, and the gap between the man in second and me stayed steady at roughly 10 metres for most of the run. I was working, but I was not chasing anything down, and nobody behind me seemed to be closing quickly.
That changed near the end. A runner who had been sitting in fourth came past fast and finished a few seconds ahead of me. I had nothing left to respond with, so the only thing to do was keep moving and get to the line.
I finished in 20:54.
That was a little slower than the same race three weeks earlier, but the context matters. With a bit more freshness and without the stomach issues, I think I could have improved on the previous run. Even so, this still did the job: it gave me a hard, honest effort on the new power meter and a useful baseline for the next block.


What the Data Says
The headline result was slightly slower than last time, but the pacing was more stable. There was still a dip towards the end, especially when I could not respond to the late pass, but the effort looks controlled rather than chaotic.

Takeaways
This was not a race I had circled in the calendar, but it was still useful.
The time was slightly slower than three weeks earlier, and I did not feel great on the day. But as a controlled hard effort for the Stryd power meter, it was exactly what I needed. The main positive is that the pacing was a little more stable, even if the finish lacked the extra gear I would have liked.
The next step is to use this as the new reference point rather than reading too much into a five-second difference on a day when I was not especially fresh.


Coach review
From a coaching standpoint, this was a very strong and well-executed 5K. The power profile shows a controlled effort with a slight positive split (353 → 334W), which is typical and acceptable, especially given the early pacing. More importantly, there was no late-race collapse, indicating good durability and that your threshold is well-aligned with your current fitness. The average power around ~340W gives us a reliable anchor for your current performance level and confirms that your Critical Power was slightly underestimated.
The key takeaway is that your sustainable 5K power sits closer to ~335–340W, with optimal execution likely achieved by slightly moderating the first kilometer. This result provides a clean benchmark to recalibrate your zones and, more importantly, defines a precise target range for race execution moving forward—particularly for the run leg of a sprint triathlon, where we’ll aim to translate this into a controlled ~310–315W off the bike.

Competing at the World Triathlon Championships is one of the highest honours for any age-group athlete.

Competing at the World Triathlon Championships is one of the highest honours for any age-group athlete.
But unlike professional or Olympic racers, there’s no financial support from the federation — every athlete covers their own costs: registration, uniforms, travel, accommodation, and more.
Below, I’ve broken down the main expenses into three categories: mandatory, travel, and optional expenses.

Mandatory expenses are those you must commit to no matter what. Photo by Emil Kalibradov on Unsplash

First of all, you need to qualify, so you will have to pay for at least one race and to register your EOI. One of the requirements is to be in “good standing” with the federation. In plain English, you need to be a member Triathlon Canada and one of the affiliate branches.
After you qualified you will need to pay a team management fee, get insurance, register for your race, purchase the race gear, and finally the mandatory parade gear.
Note that I took part in two event: the individual sprint race and the mixed team relay race. Your cost here will vary, depend on which events you will actually compete in.

💡 If you already own a recent Team Canada kit, you may be allowed to race in it, saving a few hundred dollars.

Putting the bike on a plane can be expensive.


You qualified and you have all the gear needed! Congratulations! Now you need to get to the race venue. Of course, this category will be vastly dependent on how far you need to travel, your travel and accommodation preferences, even the kind of race you do (do you need to take the bike on a plane or not?). In my case I booked the flight with FlightHub ad the accommodation for 6 nights with Nirvana. I am sure you can find cheaper accommodation, but Nirvana made it easier because they also included shuttle to and from the airport, and the bike tune up. All of those were extras to the basic accommodation deal, but booking everything through the same website, at the same time, made it very convenient and it gave me piece of mind.
Because I was travelling to Australia through US I had to get an electronic VISA for both countries.
I then decided to bring my own bike rather than rent one in Wollongong. First of all, I felt like I “owed” it my bike to take it to the race: it gets me the qualification, it deserved the race! Furthermore, it quickly became obvious to whoever was trying to rent a bike that availability was very limited. Regardless, taking the bike on the plane means having to pay the corresponding extra charge.
Another thing I got before actually travelling to Australia was an e-sim. I got it with HolaFly and it was money well spent, as it allows me to always be in touch with Team Canada in Slack wherever I was.
The next expense if food. This will be drastically different for everyone. In my case I had some food and snacks at the airport, and when in Wollongong I only purchased food at supermarkets and ate in my hotel room. Just trying to save some money really.
The final expense was gifts. After such a long journey, you will want to show some appreciation to whoever supported you and stayed back home.

title: The Cost of Racing the World Championships
text:
Final thoughts
The experience of racing at Worlds comes with a significant price tag, but also with an immeasurable reward — representing your country, sharing the course with athletes from around the world, and closing a long chapter of hard work and dedication.
It’s not just an investment in a single race — it’s an investment in a lifelong memory.



I’ll never forget Wollongong and the Team Canada experience.
